introduction: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá admired the railways, the telegraph and the schools of his age, urged the Persians to learn from them, and foresaw that people would one day fly from city to city as easily as they took a carriage. These passages praise material progress, describe a century unlike any before it, and name what makes advancement humane: justice, education, unity, and a spiritual civilization to match the material one, without which the same inventions serve war. Ninety-one outside voices stand beside them: Genesis and Job on dominion and wisdom, the Qur’an on the bounty of the earth, Sophocles' ode to man, Bacon, Tennyson and Whitman, who shared the hope; and Thoreau, Blake, Wordsworth, Emerson, Gandhi and the Tao Te Ching, who counted the cost.
questions: What, in these passages, makes material progress good, and what makes it dangerous? Compare Thoreau's "improved means to an unimproved end."
Tennyson saw the skies filled with commerce and Whitman saw God's purpose in the cable and the canal. What has happened to that hope since, and what in these readings still stands?
"Distance is annihilated." The Tao Te Ching imagined neighbours who never visit. What is gained and what is lost when the world becomes one place?
Job describes the miner's skill and asks where wisdom is to be found. What is the "spiritual civilization" that these talks say has been neglected?
One talk puts spiritual progress first and material after; Confucius said, enrich them and then teach them. Does the order matter?
Dickens called his age the best of times and the worst of times. How would you describe the present one in the terms of this guide?

Wilfred Owen wrote from the trenches of the first war fought with the new weapons.
Isaiah looks to a day when nations beat their swords into ploughshares.

Tennyson cried: forward, forward let us range; let the great world spin for ever down the ringing grooves of change.
